title: Kiwi — 8yo African grey: collapse and twitching on the cage floor
presentation: 8-year-old female African grey parrot, found on the cage floor twitching this morning, and now weak and unable to perch. Fed a seed mix with fruit, kept indoors behind glass with no ultraviolet light.

stages.title: Read the presentation
stages.briefing: Weight 402 g, BCS 3/5. Weak, unable to grip the perch, intermittent whole-body tremors, one witnessed seizure lasting 30 seconds. Mucous membranes pink. No head trauma, no toxin access reported, no metal ornaments or costume jewellery in the cage. Diet: sunflower-based seed mix with apple and grape, no pellets, no cuttlefish. Housed indoors behind window glass, no UV lamp. Droppings normal.
stages.prompt: Which findings direct you towards a metabolic cause?

options.label: Seizures with generalised weakness in an adult African grey
options.detail: The species and syndrome that go together

options.label: An all-seed diet with no mineral or pellet source
options.detail: A calcium-poor ration

options.label: Housed behind glass with no ultraviolet light
options.detail: No route to vitamin D3 synthesis

options.label: Normal droppings
options.detail: Reassuring about the gut, silent on the brain

options.label: No metal ornaments in the cage
options.detail: Worth asking, but owners miss the source

stages.explanation: African greys have a species-specific hypocalcaemic syndrome, and the history here supplies both halves of it: a seed diet with no calcium and no ultraviolet exposure to activate what little vitamin D there is. The owner’s confidence that there is no metal in the cage is worth recording and not relying on — heavy metal is the other differential and owners routinely overlook the source.

stages.title: Choose the tests
stages.briefing: The parrot is stabilised in an incubator with oxygen. You can take a small blood volume and radiograph.

options.label: Ionised calcium
options.detail: The measurement that matters in this syndrome

options.label: Total calcium with albumin and phosphorus
options.detail: Interprets the total against protein binding

options.label: Whole-body radiographs
options.detail: Metal density in the gizzard, and bone quality

options.label: Blood lead and zinc concentrations
options.detail: The differential that must be excluded

options.label: Haematology and biochemistry with uric acid
options.detail: Renal and hepatic screening in a collapsed bird

options.label: Cerebrospinal fluid collection
options.detail: Not practicable or justifiable in a 400 g parrot

options.label: Chlamydia psittaci PCR as the first-line test
options.detail: A sensible screen in a sick parrot, but it does not explain seizures with this history

stages.explanation: Ionised calcium is the test the diagnosis rests on: an African grey can seizure with a total calcium that reads borderline, and only the ionised fraction reflects what the neurones see. Radiographs and heavy metal concentrations are run in the same visit because lead and zinc produce the same neurological picture and demand entirely different treatment.

stages.title: Interpret the results
stages.briefing: Ionised calcium 0.62 mmol/L (ref 1.0–1.4). Total calcium 1.68 mmol/L (ref 2.1–2.6), albumin 14 g/L, phosphorus 1.9 mmol/L. Radiographs: no metallic densities in the ventriculus; generalised reduced bone opacity with thin cortices. Blood lead <0.05 ppm, zinc within reference. Uric acid 380 µmol/L (normal), glucose 14 mmol/L (normal for a parrot). Haematology unremarkable. Vitamin D3 low.
stages.prompt: Which conclusions do these results support?

options.label: Severe ionised hypocalcaemia explains the seizures
options.detail: Ionised calcium 0.62 mmol/L

options.label: Nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism with poor bone mineralisation
options.detail: Thin cortices and reduced bone opacity with low vitamin D3

options.label: Heavy metal toxicosis is excluded
options.detail: No metal on radiographs, lead and zinc within reference

options.label: Hypoalbuminaemia alone accounts for the low total calcium
options.detail: It lowers the total, but the ionised fraction is genuinely low too

options.label: Renal disease is driving the calcium loss
options.detail: Uric acid is normal

stages.explanation: This is the case that teaches why ionised calcium exists: a total of 1.68 mmol/L in a bird with an albumin of 14 g/L could have been dismissed as a protein artefact, and the ionised value shows it is not. The radiographs do double duty — they exclude heavy metal and reveal the chronic bone disease behind an apparently acute collapse.

stages.title: Commit to a diagnosis
stages.briefing: Ionised calcium 0.62 mmol/L, low vitamin D3, demineralised bone, no metal on radiographs, normal lead and zinc, all-seed diet with no ultraviolet exposure.

options.label: Hypocalcaemic syndrome of African greys from nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism
options.detail: Ionised hypocalcaemia with the diet and husbandry that caused it

options.label: Lead toxicosis
options.detail: Excluded by radiographs and blood lead

options.label: Idiopathic epilepsy
options.detail: Does not explain an ionised calcium of 0.62 mmol/L

options.label: Hepatic encephalopathy
options.detail: Liver markers and uric acid are normal

options.label: Zinc toxicosis
options.detail: Zinc within reference and no metal density

stages.explanation: The immediate treatment is parenteral calcium, but the diagnosis is about the next twelve months: conversion to a formulated diet, a UV-emitting lamp, and vitamin D3 supplementation with rechecks, because the bones are already thin. Owners who hear only "low calcium" go back to the seed mix.
